title: Chapter 47
text: i swear to god if i’m still making smoothies for a living 3 months from now i’m going to freakin…get up and keep going to work because i don’t have a safety net that affords me the ability to quit a fruitless, unfulfilling, stagnant job in pursuit of my dreams. 53 — WHEN I READ Selvin’s descriptions of the 1930s longshoremen before the strike, who lived unprotected from the vicissitudes of capital and “put up with round-the-clock shifts, cut short rest periods between jobs, and missed meal periods,” I’m reminded not only of today’s “new contract” and Talia Jane’s plight, but of a particular group of people: my students. Back in 2013, students in my first art classes at Stanford were surprised that I didn’t know about “Stanford duck syndrome.” This phrase, which imagines students as placid-seeming ducks paddling strenuously beneath the water, is essentially a joke about isolated struggle in an atmosphere obsessed with performance. In “Duck syndrome and a culture of misery,” Stanford Daily writer Tiger Sun describes seeing a friend pull two consecutive all-nighters on her birthday weekend. Sun and his friends grow concerned when they notice her face is flushed, so they take her temperature: 102.1 degrees. But when they implore her to stop, she keeps working. Sun writes:
